incidents.summary: Channel File 291 Rapid Response Content: the IPC Template Type declared 21 input parameters while sensor code supplied 20. Earlier instances wildcarded the 21st field, masking the mismatch. Two new non-wildcard instances caused an out-of-bounds read and kernel crash. The RCA states the defect evaded multiple layers of build validation.

A WAF Managed Rule containing a nested regex construct caused catastrophic PCRE backtracking; CPU reached ~100% fleet-wide, ~80% of traffic returned 502. Rules ship globally in one push by design, bypassing the normal DOG/PIG/Canary/Global stages. A regex CPU guard had been inadvertently removed in an earlier refactor.

A Bot Management feature file more than doubled in size after an upstream permissions change added duplicate column metadata. The FL2 proxy preallocates a hard 200-feature limit; the oversized file caused a Rust panic and 5xx. Regeneration every ~5 minutes against partially-updated ClickHouse nodes produced oscillation that looked like an attack.

incidents.summary: New RLP code was deployed to 7 of 8 SMARS servers; the 8th retained dormant legacy "Power Peg" code keyed to a repurposed flag. Activating the flag ran the legacy logic. Over 4 million executions in 154 stocks; loss "over $460 million" in ~45 minutes. Warning emails existed but "Knight did not design these types of messages to be system alerts".

Azure Front Door: customer configuration changes made across different control-plane versions produced incompatible metadata, exposing a latent data-plane bug that crashed asynchronous processing at edge sites. ~8.5 hours; the Last Known Good configuration was itself contaminated and had to be manually edited.

leading_indicators.signal: Deployed-version inventory versus intended-version inventory
Presence of more than one control-plane version writing the same state

observable_symptoms: A minority of hosts behaving anomalously while the majority are healthy
Aberrant output from one host that the monitoring treats as noise
Data-plane crashes triggered by metadata written by a different control-plane version
preconditions: No post-deployment verification that every target received the new artefact
Reuse of a flag, field or identifier whose meaning changed between versions
Control-plane writes that are not version-tagged

known_limits: Requires an authoritative inventory of intended state
Does not detect semantic incompatibility between two versions that are both "intended"
predictive_monitoring.rationale: Version skew is directly observable. A reconciliation check comparing intended and actual artefact per target detects it before the flag is flipped.

patterns.problem_and_mechanism: A release reaches some but not all targets, or two control-plane versions write incompatible state. The fleet then contains hosts behaving on different assumptions. The classic catastrophic form is a flag whose meaning differs between versions: setting it activates new behaviour on updated hosts and dormant legacy behaviour on the stale one.

remediations.failure_mode_if_wrong: Deploying to a target mid-incident can widen the fault

Contaminated objects identifiable
remediations.verification: Data-plane crash rate drops; repaired config validates against both versions

Version tag on every control-plane-written config object

rollback_and_escalation.escalation_trigger: Any target that cannot be reconciled to a known version
rollback_and_escalation.rollback_notes: Rolling back cannot fix a host that never received the change; and rollback may reintroduce the legacy path

root_causes: Deployment tooling reports success without verifying per-target state
Repurposing a flag rather than retiring it
No compatibility contract between control-plane versions
patterns.title: Partial deployment and version skew
verification: Version inventory must reconcile to 100%, not "no failures observed"
Confirm the last-known-good artefact is genuinely clean before restoring it

automation_safety_limits: Automated rollback is unsafe once the new version has written persistent state in a new format
Automation must be able to distinguish "rollout progressing" from "rollout progressing into failure"
diagnostic_methods: Segment errors by version pair; if errors concentrate on the mixed pair, this is the pattern
Halt the rollout and observe whether errors stabilise at the current mix
Reproduce on a small cluster — Zhang et al. found all 123 upgrade failures reproduce on three nodes or fewer, 57% on one

incidents.summary: During a Kubernetes 1.24 upgrade the deprecated node-role.kubernetes.io/master label was removed. BGP route-reflector pods selected on that label, so route propagation broke cluster-wide, surfacing first as API-server admission-webhook timeouts. 314 minutes; prolonged because the configuration was undocumented and the restore runbook untested.

leading_indicators.signal: Cross-version interaction error rate during the upgrade window

observable_symptoms: Errors concentrated on interactions that cross the version boundary
Cluster-wide degradation disproportionate to the fraction upgraded
preconditions: Rolling upgrade with mixed versions serving simultaneously
Shared persistent state or wire protocol between versions
No explicit cross-version compatibility test

known_limits: Requires version-pair segmentation in telemetry, which most systems do not emit
Semantic incompatibility produces correct-looking messages with wrong meaning
predictive_monitoring.rationale: The incompatibility is detectable within minutes of the first mixed interaction, but there is no signal before the first mixed interaction occurs.

patterns.problem_and_mechanism: During a rolling upgrade two versions coexist and interact. Zhang et al. found about two-thirds of upgrade failures are caused by incompatible interaction between two software versions — a failure mode invisible to single-version testing. Incompatibility centres on persistent data and network messages; mostly syntactic, but a substantial third is semantic, where the format is unchanged and the meaning is not.

remediations.action: Halt the rollout at the current mix
remediations.blast_radius: Upgrade stalls; both versions remain in service
remediations.failure_mode_if_wrong: Leaves the cluster in a mixed state indefinitely, which is itself the failing condition
preconditions: Rollout can be paused without leaving state inconsistent
remediations.verification: Error rate stops growing

remediations.failure_mode_if_wrong: Rolling back past a persistent-state format change can corrupt or strand data
preconditions: Persistent state written by the new version is readable by the old, or vice versa
remediations.verification: All nodes on one version; cross-version error class disappears

required_telemetry.signal: Error rate segmented by (caller version, callee version)
Upgrade progress — fraction of nodes on each version

root_causes: Persistent-data or message-format change without a compatibility window
Semantic change to an unchanged field
Testing only single-version and fully-upgraded states, never the mixed state
patterns.title: Rolling upgrade incompatibility between coexisting versions
verification: Confirm zero nodes remain on the intermediate version
Validate persistent state written during the mixed window is readable by the surviving version

diagnostic_methods: Compare rollout timeline against cache/TTL expiry; progressive spread implicates TTL masking
Check whether the new version has written state the old version must read

evidence.citation: OpenAI incident, 11 December 2024

incidents.summary: A new telemetry service made every node perform Kubernetes API operations whose cost scaled with cluster size, overwhelming API servers. Per-node DNS caching delayed visible failure long enough for the rollout to continue; as cached records expired over ~20 minutes, services failed fleet-wide. Engineers then needed control-plane access to remove the service but could not obtain it because of the API load.

leading_indicators.signal: Longest TTL or cache lifetime between a change and its observable effect
Time since the rollback path was last exercised

observable_symptoms: Failure appears minutes to hours after the rollout appeared successful
Failure spreads progressively as cached records expire, rather than all at once
Rollback attempt fails or produces new errors
preconditions: A change that writes state or alters a schema
Caches or TTLs between the change and the observable symptom
Rollback procedure not exercised recently

known_limits: Requires an inventory of every cache and TTL in the dependency path, which is rarely complete
predictive_monitoring.rationale: Both the TTL-masking window and rollback-path staleness are directly computable. Neither requires a model.

patterns.problem_and_mechanism: The standard remedy for a bad change is to reverse it. Three things defeat this. First, the change wrote state the previous version cannot read. Second, caching or TTLs delay the failure signal until the rollout has passed the point where rollback is cheap. Third, the rollback path itself is cold — untested, and therefore not trustworthy at the moment it is needed.

remediations.action: Roll back immediately on suspicion, before diagnosis
remediations.blast_radius: Service returns to the previous version
remediations.failure_mode_if_wrong: Rollback may reintroduce a security vulnerability the change fixed
preconditions: Rollback is easy, trusted and recently exercised
No persistent-state barrier
remediations.verification: SLI recovers; version inventory confirms rollback completed

remediations.blast_radius: Privileged access granted outside normal authentication
remediations.failure_mode_if_wrong: Break-glass credentials are a standing privilege-escalation risk if not tightly governed
preconditions: Break-glass credentials exist offline and have been exercised
remediations.verification: Offending workload removed; control-plane load recovers

required_telemetry.signal: Rollout progress versus cache/TTL expiry horizon
Date of last successful rollback exercise per service

rollback_and_escalation.escalation_trigger: Rollback attempted and did not restore the SLI
rollback_and_escalation.rollback_notes: Google CRE's doctrine is rollback-first; its stated precondition is that rollbacks are "easy to perform; and trusted to be low-risk", maintained by rolling back periodically "just because". Its stated exception is schema/data migration.

Schema or data migration coupled to a binary release
Rollback treated as an exception path rather than a routine one
patterns.title: Rollback unavailable, unsafe, or masked past the safe point

incidents.summary: A script intended to remove a legacy app was passed site IDs instead of app IDs; the deletion API "accepts both site and app identifiers and assumes the input is correct". 883 sites deleted across 775 customers in 23 minutes, with no engineering alert. First restoration 8 April, complete 18 April — up to 14 days.

observable_symptoms: Large-scale resource deletion following a normal-looking workflow, generating no alerts

No soft-delete or staged confirmation
A reconciler that treats an empty or malformed desired state as authoritative

patterns.problem_and_mechanism: An automated process executes a destructive operation across a scope far larger than intended, because the scope was supplied incorrectly and nothing validated it. observable_symptoms: Simultaneous failure across environments that share no infrastructure
Onset clustered at a vendor-default maintenance window
Node-level connectivity loss immediately after a package restart

Emergency-change procedures with fewer approvals and no staged rollout
Shared base images or defaults across otherwise independent environments

Requires image-build visibility that many organisations do not maintain

patterns.problem_and_mechanism: A security update, emergency mitigation or hardening change breaks the system it protects. The distinguishing feature is that the change arrives under time pressure or outside normal change control, so the usual staging and review are compressed or absent. A common sub-shape is an automatic OS security-update channel that the platform team does not know is enabled.

preconditions: Alternative patching path exists

remediations.action: Reconfigure the component to preserve the state it destroyed
remediations.failure_mode_if_wrong: A wrong configuration can break networking on restart in a different way
preconditions: Root mechanism understood
remediations.verification: Package restart in a canary no longer removes routes

Enabled update channels and their windows

Emergency-change path deliberately bypassing staged rollout
A mitigation changing a resource limit or disabling a component whose failure path is untested
patterns.title: Security patch or mitigation as the outage cause
verification: Restart the component deliberately in a canary and confirm the destructive behaviour is gone
Audit for other update channels with the same property — Datadog's stated remediation

Retry-budget changes affect every client and cannot be safely rolled out fleet-wide without staging
diagnostic_methods: Compare server-observed request rate with independently measured client demand; a large gap is the signature
Segment traffic into first attempts and retries — if retries dominate, this is the pattern
Remove load and observe: if the system does not recover, it is metastable (F2.6), not merely overloaded

incidents.summary: An automated scaling activity triggered unexpected client behaviour inside the internal network; the resulting connection surge congested networking devices. A latent client back-off defect, in production for years and never exposed, prevented self-recovery. Internal monitoring was impaired, delaying root-cause identification.

A brief network disruption caused storage servers to re-request membership data from the metadata service. Global Secondary Index adoption had grown membership lists, pushing requests near the timeout threshold; requests timed out, servers retried, load compounded. Escape required pausing metadata requests to shed load.

leading_indicators.signal: Ratio of retried to original requests, per layer
Queue length relative to thread-pool size — Google SRE guidance is to keep it at 50% or less

observable_symptoms: Request rate at the server far exceeding originating client demand
Latency and error rate stay elevated after the triggering fault has cleared
Queue depth growing monotonically
preconditions: Retries without a budget, cap, or randomised exponential backoff
Retries implemented at more than one layer of the call stack
Capacity headroom smaller than the amplification factor

known_limits: Bronson et al. note a system can sit in the vulnerable phase indefinitely with no symptom and no load increase
Requires retries to be distinguishable from first attempts in telemetry, which many stacks do not emit
predictive_monitoring.rationale: The retry ratio and queue-depth-to-pool-size ratio rise measurably before collapse, giving minutes of warning. But the vulnerable state can persist for months with no visible signal, so this is early detection rather than prediction.

patterns.problem_and_mechanism: A transient fault causes clients to retry. Retries add load, which lengthens latency, which causes more timeouts, which causes more retries. The feedback loop sustains the failure after the original trigger is gone. Huang et al. found retry policy to be the sustaining effect in more than 50% of studied metastable incidents. Amplification multiplies when retries occur at several layers of the stack independently.

remediations.action: Shed load — reject a defined fraction of requests to break the feedback loop
remediations.blast_radius: A defined fraction of requests fail fast
remediations.failure_mode_if_wrong: Shedding on a false signal causes an avoidable outage; shedding too little does nothing
preconditions: Shedding path exists and has been exercised
Clients handle 503 without amplifying further
remediations.verification: Queue depth falls; latency recovers; retry ratio normalises

remediations.action: Disable the triggering automated activity
remediations.failure_mode_if_wrong: Halting scaling during genuine demand growth creates a capacity shortfall
preconditions: Triggering activity identified
remediations.verification: Connection rate stops growing

remediations.action: Deploy retry budgets and randomised exponential backoff
remediations.failure_mode_if_wrong: Over-tight budgets drop legitimate retries and reduce availability
preconditions: Client code can be changed — often it cannot; see F2.2
remediations.verification: Retry ratio bounded under induced fault

required_telemetry.signal: Retry counters distinguishable from first attempts
Queue depth and thread-pool utilisation
Per-connection cancellation rate

rollback_and_escalation.escalation_trigger: System does not recover when the trigger is removed

root_causes: Unbounded retries
Fixed-interval retries producing synchronised waves
A latent client back-off defect that only manifests under an unusual event
patterns.title: Retry amplification
verification: Confirm recovery survives removal of the mitigation; a system that re-enters the loop when shedding stops has not recovered
Watch the backlog drain as a second load event — Datadog measured recovery throughput at twice normal

automation_safety_limits: Automated recovery must re-admit traffic in increments; restoring everything at once is the documented second failure
Autoscaling is not a mitigation here and can be an amplifier (see F11.1)
diagnostic_methods: Plot arrival-time distribution; clustering at a period is the signature
Check whether the spike coincides with a restart of the service the clients depend on
Distinguish retries from new requests — Cloudflare's stated remediation includes adding request metadata to do exactly this

incidents.summary: The first working day after the holiday break: client caches were cold and clients pulled more data than usual. An AWS Transit Gateway could not scale fast enough; packet loss saturated the web tier. Recovery then failed on its own limits — provision-service hit the Linux open-files limit and an AWS quota while adding 1,200 servers. Message success fell from >99.999% to ~99%.

A React useEffect dependency-array bug made the dashboard re-issue an /organizations call on every state change. Because the Tenant Service authorises all API requests, its overload returned 5xx across the API surface; restarting it caused every dashboard to re-authenticate simultaneously — an explicit thundering herd amplified by the client bug.

Netgear routers with a hard-coded NTP server IP polled at one-second intervals until answered, with no backoff — so refusing to answer increased the load. Flawed clients were present in over 2,400 autonomous systems. The defining property is that the victim cannot fix the clients and cannot make the load stop by failing.

leading_indicators.signal: Concentration of client refresh/retry timestamps (clustering rather than uniformity)
Known calendar events — holidays, scheduled windows, mass TTL expiry

observable_symptoms: Request rate spike with a sharp edge at a round time or immediately after a restart
Recovery attempts causing a second, larger spike
Load that does not correlate with user-visible demand
preconditions: Clients that retry or refresh on a shared schedule with no jitter
A recovery path that re-admits all clients simultaneously
Cache TTLs that expire together

known_limits: Cannot predict herds caused by an unplanned restart of a dependency
Cannot fix clients that are not yours
predictive_monitoring.rationale: Calendar-driven herds are fully predictable — Slack's own remediation is to request capacity increases ahead of the holiday period. Clustering in arrival-time distribution is directly measurable before it becomes a spike.

patterns.problem_and_mechanism: A population of clients acts simultaneously, producing a load spike far above steady state. The synchronising clock may be a real clock (a cron window, a TTL expiry, midnight), a shared event (a service restarting and every session re-authenticating at once), or a calendar (the first working day after a holiday, when every client cache is cold). The hardest variant is when the clients cannot be fixed because they are not yours.

remediations.action: Staged re-admission of traffic in increments
remediations.blast_radius: Clients admitted in tranches; the remainder stay unserved longer
remediations.failure_mode_if_wrong: Increments too large re-trigger collapse; too small prolongs the outage
preconditions: A traffic-steering control exists
Increment size and interval defined in advance
remediations.verification: Each increment stabilises before the next is admitted

remediations.action: Pre-scale ahead of a known calendar event
remediations.failure_mode_if_wrong: Wasted spend; and the wrong component scaled leaves the real bottleneck
preconditions: Event is known in advance
Capacity can be reserved
remediations.verification: Load test against the predicted spike shape

remediations.action: Introduce client-side randomised delay
remediations.failure_mode_if_wrong: Not applicable where clients cannot be upgraded — the defining hard case
preconditions: Clients are under your control
remediations.verification: Arrival-time distribution flattens

required_telemetry.signal: Request arrival-time distribution, not just rate
Retry versus new-request discrimination

rollback_and_escalation.escalation_trigger: Recovery attempt produces a larger spike than the original event

root_causes: No randomised jitter on client refresh or retry
Recovery that restores all clients at once rather than in increments
A client bug that turns normal state changes into repeated requests
patterns.title: Thundering herd and synchronised client behaviour
verification: Confirm arrival-time distribution is spread, not merely that the rate is lower
Verify the recovery path itself was load-tested — Slack's stated remediation is to load-test provision-service regularly

automation_safety_limits: Automated discard is irreversible and must be gated, regardless of how clear the signal is
Automatically adding consumer capacity can worsen a downstream bottleneck that is the real constraint
diagnostic_methods: Distinguish "producer up" from "consumer down" by comparing both rates, not lag alone
Check item age at processing; high age with normal rate means the backlog is old, not growing
For serverless, check invocation lineage — AWS Lambda increments a lineage counter and drops requests after 16 invocations of the same event

evidence.citation: Datadog, deep dive into platform-level impact of the 2023-03-08 incident
AWS, Summary of the Amazon EC2 and Amazon RDS Service Disruption, April 2011
AWS, Detecting and stopping recursive loops in Lambda functions

incidents.summary: During recovery, traffic went from hundreds of millions of packets per second to almost zero, then to roughly twice usual throughput while processing the backlog. Datadog prioritised real-time data processing ahead of historical backfill.

EBS nodes searching simultaneously for re-mirroring space exhausted free capacity and entered continuous search loops. The EBS control plane had a long timeout, so queued create-volume requests backed up and caused thread starvation; once the regional thread pool filled, API requests failed across all AZs despite physical isolation.

leading_indicators.signal: Consumer lag trend and its derivative
Producer rate divided by consumer rate sustained above 1
Invocation lineage depth (detecting a function feeding its own trigger)

observable_symptoms: Queue depth or consumer lag growing monotonically
Items processed long after they were relevant
Recovery throughput significantly above steady state as the backlog drains
preconditions: Queue with no depth bound or with a bound larger than useful
Consumers whose throughput can fall below producer rate
No age-based discard for work that is no longer useful

known_limits: A queue that has been absorbing imbalance for a long time gives a misleadingly healthy instantaneous reading
Segment-based retention means low-traffic topics retain data longer than configured, distorting expiry estimates
predictive_monitoring.rationale: Lag trend plus producer/consumer rate ratio gives a computable time-to-exhaustion for retention or memory. This is arithmetic, not inference.

patterns.problem_and_mechanism: Work arrives faster than it is consumed and accumulates. The queue absorbs the imbalance for a while, which hides it, then the accumulated work becomes its own problem: memory pressure, timeouts on items that have aged out, and a recovery load spike when the backlog finally drains. A self-feeding variant occurs when a consumer's output is written back to its own input.

remediations.action: Prioritise real-time processing over backfill
remediations.failure_mode_if_wrong: Discarding work that was actually needed
preconditions: Work can be classified as current versus historical
remediations.verification: Current-data freshness recovers while backlog drains separately

remediations.action: Set concurrency to zero or disable the event-source mapping to halt a recursive loop
remediations.failure_mode_if_wrong: Halting a legitimate high-volume function stops real work
preconditions: Loop positively identified by lineage depth
remediations.verification: Invocation rate returns to zero; queue depth stops growing

remediations.action: Shed or age out stale work
remediations.failure_mode_if_wrong: Irreversible data loss — GitHub dropped ~200,000 webhook payloads that exceeded TTL
preconditions: Work has a defined expiry semantics
remediations.verification: Queue depth falls; no downstream expects the discarded items

required_telemetry.signal: Queue depth and consumer lag per partition
Producer and consumer rates
Item age at processing time

rollback_and_escalation.escalation_trigger: Lag growth continues after consumer capacity is added
rollback_and_escalation.rollback_notes: Discarded work cannot be recovered; this is the one irreversible remediation in the pattern

root_causes: Consumer slowdown from a downstream dependency
Producer surge
Recursive invocation — output written to the source rather than the destination
Poison message blocking a partition
patterns.title: Queue backlog and unbounded growth
verification: Confirm lag returns to baseline and stays there through at least one peak cycle
Plan for the drain as a second load event, not as recovery

automation_safety_limits: Automatically enlarging the pool pushes the wall outward and can move the failure to memory or to the dependency
Automated failover is not safe here by default; the trigger conditions overlap with network partition
diagnostic_methods: Confirm pool utilisation at 100% with healthy CPU/memory — this distinguishes the pattern from ordinary overload
Trace what the held slots are waiting on
Check whether the pool's scope is wider than the fault's scope

incidents.summary: A feature-flag bug from the previous day's migration stopped schema-cache writes; the cache that shielded the database starved, ingest queried MySQL directly at greatly increased rates, hitting a rare internal race that locked thread after thread until the connection pool was exhausted. 68-minute total outage. The stated leading indicator was an internal SLO slowly burning for hours after the migration.

A long control-plane timeout caused queued create-volume requests to exhaust the regional thread pool, so API requests failed across all availability zones in the region despite physical isolation between them.

leading_indicators.signal: Pool utilisation and wait time, trended
Mean work-item duration — rising duration at constant rate predicts exhaustion

observable_symptoms: New requests rejected or queued while CPU and memory appear healthy
Pool utilisation pinned at 100%
Failures spreading to callers that share the pool but not the fault
preconditions: A fixed-size pool
Work items whose duration can grow without bound (long timeouts, lock waits)
Pool shared across a wider scope than the fault domain

known_limits: Utilisation can be healthy right up to a step change in dependency latency
Does not distinguish a legitimate demand increase from a dependency slowdown without the duration signal
predictive_monitoring.rationale: Pool exhaustion is a resource with a hard limit and an observable consumption rate, so time-to-exhaustion is arithmetic. Google SRE's queue-length-below-50%-of-pool-size guidance gives a concrete threshold.

patterns.problem_and_mechanism: A bounded pool of connections, threads or workers is fully consumed, so new work cannot be served regardless of how much CPU or memory is free. The pool is frequently exhausted not by demand but by each unit of work taking longer — a slow dependency, a lock, or a long timeout converts a throughput problem into a hard capacity wall. Regional pooling turns a local problem into a regional one.

remediations.action: Circuit-break to protect the exhausted resource
remediations.failure_mode_if_wrong: Breaking on a false signal causes an avoidable outage
preconditions: Circuit breaker exists
Callers handle rejection
remediations.verification: Pool utilisation falls below threshold; dependency recovers

remediations.action: Fail over to a replica
remediations.blast_radius: All traffic moves to the replica
remediations.failure_mode_if_wrong: Failover under partition risks split-brain — see F4.1
preconditions: Replica is current
Failover has been exercised
remediations.verification: Pool recovers on the new primary; no write divergence

remediations.action: Reduce dependency timeouts so slots are released sooner
remediations.failure_mode_if_wrong: Timeouts too short convert slow successes into failures and can increase retries (F2.1)
preconditions: Shorter timeout does not break legitimate slow operations
remediations.verification: Pool wait time falls under the same load

required_telemetry.signal: Pool size, in-use count, and wait queue length
Work-item duration distribution

rollback_and_escalation.escalation_trigger: Pool exhaustion recurs after the apparent cause is removed

root_causes: Long timeouts on a dependency holding pool slots
Lock contention in a downstream store
Loss of a cache that previously absorbed the work (see F4.5)
Regional rather than per-zone pool scoping
patterns.title: Connection, thread or worker-pool exhaustion
verification: Pool utilisation returns to normal headroom under representative load, not just at reduced load
Confirm the underlying holder of slots is resolved, not merely that the pool drained

automation_safety_limits: A kill switch is the only safe automated action here; automated failover to larger instances made Figma's incident worse
The automated action must not require the saturated hosts to respond, or it cannot execute
diagnostic_methods: CPU profiling to attribute saturation to a module — Cloudflare identified the WAF this way within ~18 minutes
Test the suspect rule against adversarial input offline, measuring step count
Confirm the failure is fleet-simultaneous, which rules out capacity and infrastructure causes

incidents.summary: A new XSS WAF rule containing a nested construct caused exponential PCRE backtracking. CPU reached ~100% fleet-wide and traffic dropped ~80%. A CPU guard had been inadvertently removed in an earlier refactor. Recovery was a global kill switch at 14:07 UTC; CPU normalised at 14:09.

An ElastiCache cluster-bus pub/sub buffer grew exponentially when messages could not be delivered fast enough, and the buffer-truncation routine used an expensive memmove, creating a runaway CPU feedback loop. Four incidents over ~11 hours; alerting fired within seconds on 100% engine CPU. Initial failover to larger clusters made it worse.

leading_indicators.signal: CPU time per rule or per operation, measured in CI against adversarial inputs
Presence of nested quantifiers or unbounded backtracking constructs in a rule

observable_symptoms: CPU at or near 100% across the whole fleet simultaneously
Large-scale 5xx with no infrastructure fault
Synthetic monitoring failing before customer reports
preconditions: User- or tenant-influenced input reaching an unbounded-complexity operation
No CPU-time guard or execution budget on the operation
Rules or code deployed fleet-wide without staged rollout

known_limits: Requires adversarial inputs in the test corpus, not just correctness cases
Does not catch cost that only appears at production input scale
predictive_monitoring.rationale: CPU cost per rule is measurable in CI before deployment. Cloudflare's own remediation list includes CPU profiling in tests and auditing all 3,868 existing rules.

patterns.problem_and_mechanism: A single computation consumes CPU wildly out of proportion to its input size, and because the code runs on every request on every host, the entire fleet saturates at once. The canonical form is catastrophic regular-expression backtracking, where adding one character to the input multiplies the step count by an order of magnitude. A second form is an algorithmic cliff in a buffer-management routine that creates a runaway feedback loop.

remediations.action: Global kill switch disabling the offending module
remediations.failure_mode_if_wrong: Disabling a security module during an attack
preconditions: Kill switch exists and has been exercised
Module can fail open
remediations.verification: CPU returns to baseline within seconds; traffic recovers

remediations.action: Enforce a CPU-time budget per operation
remediations.failure_mode_if_wrong: Budget too tight causes legitimate operations to be abandoned silently
preconditions: Engine supports execution budgets
remediations.verification: Adversarial input no longer saturates CPU

remediations.action: Migrate to a regex engine with linear-time guarantees
remediations.failure_mode_if_wrong: Semantic differences between engines silently change detection behaviour
preconditions: Rule syntax compatible
Full rule corpus revalidated
remediations.verification: Full rule corpus produces identical match results

required_telemetry.signal: Per-host CPU utilisation with fleet-wide aggregation
CPU profile attributable to a module or rule

rollback_and_escalation.escalation_trigger: Fleet-wide CPU saturation with no traffic increase

root_causes: Regex engine with exponential worst case (PCRE) and no runtime bound
A CPU-protection guard silently removed during an earlier refactor
An expensive operation in a hot path with unbounded input growth
patterns.title: CPU exhaustion from pathological computation
verification: CPU baseline restored across every location, not just a sample
Re-enable the module only after testing; Cloudflare restored the WAF 45 minutes after the kill switch, not immediately

affected_systems: any request-serving system with retries or caches; consensus and coordination systems
automation_safety_limits: Automated capacity addition is ineffective and can be harmful; the system is not capacity-limited, it is loop-limited
Automated restart of components may re-enter the loop on cold caches (see F2.7)
Isaacs et al. (HotOS '25) state the field can recognise and reproduce metastable failures but cannot yet predict vulnerability in advance
diagnostic_methods: The definitive test: remove or sharply reduce external load. If the system does not recover, it is metastable
Identify the amplifier by comparing origin demand to backend load
Check for a recently-lost cache or a recently-changed retry policy

incidents.summary: Enabling Consul streaming plus a 50% node increase caused excessive blocking on a single Go channel, compounded by a BoltDB freelist growing to 7.8MB so that nominal 16kB Raft log writes became far larger, producing 2–3 second write latencies. 73 hours. Critical monitoring relied on the affected systems, including Consul. Player re-admission was throttled via DNS steering in 10% increments.

Congestion persisted because a latent client back-off defect prevented the system from recovering on its own; escape required disabling the scaling activity and moving internal DNS traffic off the congested paths.

leading_indicators.signal: Hidden capacity — the margin between current load and the amplified load that would occur after a fault
Work-amplification factor under induced fault (measured, not inferred)

observable_symptoms: Load stays high after the trigger ends
Reducing external demand does not restore service
Recovery requires deliberate, drastic intervention
preconditions: A work-amplifying mechanism — retries, look-aside cache, error handling
Capacity headroom smaller than the amplification factor
No load shedding or admission control

known_limits: Hidden capacity is not directly observable
Isaacs et al. propose an inflection point in the state space as a candidate early-warning signal, but this is modelling work, not a deployed capability
predictive_monitoring.rationale: The vulnerable phase is, per Bronson et al., indistinguishable from the stable phase under normal observation. There is no published method for predicting vulnerability in production.

patterns.problem_and_mechanism: A trigger pushes the system into a bad state held in place by a feedback loop. Removing the trigger does not restore service, because the sustaining effect — usually retries, sometimes a lost cache — is now generating the load itself. Bronson et al.'s key conceptual move is that the trigger is not the root cause; the sustaining effect is, and many different triggers activate the same underlying pathology. A system can sit in the vulnerable phase for months with no symptom and no load increase.

remediations.action: Aggressive load shedding to break the feedback loop
remediations.failure_mode_if_wrong: Shedding without breaking the loop achieves nothing but lost requests
preconditions: Shedding path exercised
A floor below which shedding stops
remediations.verification: Load falls below the amplification threshold and stays down when shedding is relaxed

remediations.action: Disable the amplifying feature
remediations.failure_mode_if_wrong: Disabling the wrong feature prolongs the outage while appearing to act
preconditions: Amplifier identified
Feature can be disabled without data loss
remediations.verification: Amplification factor returns to baseline under test

remediations.action: Staged re-admission of traffic after the loop is broken
remediations.failure_mode_if_wrong: Re-entering the metastable state, restarting the outage
preconditions: Traffic steering available
Increment size defined
remediations.verification: Each increment stabilises before the next

required_telemetry.signal: Offered load versus served load versus origin demand
Retry ratio and cache hit ratio together

rollback_and_escalation.escalation_trigger: Load does not fall when external demand is removed
rollback_and_escalation.rollback_notes: Rolling back the trigger does not help by definition; the sustaining effect must be addressed

root_causes: Retry policy without budget or backoff (the most common sustaining effect)
Cache loss producing query amplification against the origin
Capacity degradation amplification — the system becomes slower as it becomes busier
patterns.title: Metastable failure — the system does not recover when the trigger is removed
verification: Relax the mitigation and confirm the system stays healthy; this is the only real proof of exit
Re-admit load in increments and watch for the amplification signature returning

affected_systems: any tier restarted only in emergencies
automation_safety_limits: Automated bulk restart is the specific action that re-triggers the fault; rate limiting is mandatory, not optional
Cold-start capability cannot be verified except by exercising it, which is itself risky
diagnostic_methods: Compare actual restart progress rate against the runbook estimate early, and re-plan rather than waiting
Determine whether bulk restart re-triggers the fault; if so, serialise and accept the duration
Check whether the origin can serve cold-cache load at all

incidents.summary: S3's index and placement subsystems required full restarts; the restart plus safety checks took hours because S3 had grown substantially since these subsystems were last fully restarted. ~4h17m total.

Front-end servers had to be restarted at a rate of a few hundred per hour to avoid re-triggering the failure, making the serialised restart the dominant term in a ~17-hour recovery. AWS's remediation list includes accelerating cold-start work.
Cache redeployment from a standing start was error-prone; deployment tooling was built for incremental adjustment, not for bootstrapping a large cluster from zero.

leading_indicators.signal: Time since the last full restart of this subsystem, versus its growth since then
Measured origin load at zero cache hit ratio (tested, not modelled)

observable_symptoms: Restart takes far longer than the documented or expected time
Restarting hosts in bulk re-triggers the original failure, forcing a slow serialised restart
Origin saturates immediately when caches are empty
preconditions: The system has grown substantially since its last full restart
Deployment tooling designed for incremental change, not bootstrap
Origin capacity sized for a warm-cache hit ratio

known_limits: Predicts that the estimate is wrong, not what the correct estimate is
The only way to obtain a correct estimate is to perform the restart
predictive_monitoring.rationale: "Time since last full restart" and "growth since then" are both trivially observable and together predict that the documented restart time is stale. No model is required.

patterns.problem_and_mechanism: A system that runs well in steady state cannot come back from zero. Tooling built for incremental adjustment cannot bootstrap a large cluster; caches that were always warm must be filled from a cold origin that cannot serve the load; and subsystems that have not been fully restarted in years take far longer than anyone expects because they have grown since. The capability decays silently because it is never exercised.

remediations.action: Serialised, rate-limited restart
remediations.failure_mode_if_wrong: Rate too high re-triggers the fault and resets progress
preconditions: Rate limit derived from observed re-trigger threshold
remediations.verification: Each batch stabilises before the next

remediations.action: Warm the cache before admitting traffic
remediations.failure_mode_if_wrong: Admitting traffic to warm the cache saturates the origin
preconditions: A warming path exists that does not use production traffic
remediations.verification: Hit ratio reaches a threshold before admission

required_telemetry.signal: Last full-restart timestamp and duration per subsystem
Cache hit ratio and origin request rate

rollback_and_escalation.escalation_trigger: Restart progress rate implies a recovery time exceeding the runbook estimate by a wide margin
rollback_and_escalation.rollback_notes: There is nothing to roll back; the system is already down

root_causes: Recovery procedures never exercised at current scale
Restart cost scaling with data or fleet size while the runbook's estimate does not
Bootstrap path that does not exist because it was never needed
patterns.title: Cold-start incapacity — the system cannot restart at scale
verification: Confirm the subsystem is fully restarted, not partially; partial restarts leave inconsistent state
Track hit ratio recovery, not just error rate, before declaring normal capacity

Check resource consumption on pre-existing nodes, not only on the new ones
Verify that new nodes actually hold the data they claim to own

incidents.summary: A relatively small capacity addition to the Kinesis front-end fleet pushed servers past the OS-configured maximum thread count, because each front-end maintains threads per fleet member. Shard-map cache construction could not complete, leaving servers unable to route. Cascaded to Cognito, CloudWatch, Lambda, EventBridge, ECS and EKS.

A state-management program always sought a slot for new webapp instances before freeing slots held by departed ones. After a 75% scale-up, slots were exhausted and the program exited early, leaving HAProxy state stale for 8+ hours. The visible outage only occurred later when end-of-day scaling terminated the older instances HAProxy still believed in.

Adding six Cassandra nodes with a misunderstood auto_bootstrap setting meant new nodes served reads for partitions before receiving the data. ~9.5 hours, all services affected. Testing with one new node had hidden the bug because quorum masked it; it only appeared at six. No monitoring existed for "row not found" errors.

preconditions: Per-peer state on each node (O(N) per node, O(N²) system-wide)

Bootstrap semantics that allow serving before data transfer completes

predictive_monitoring.rationale: Per-node resource consumption as a function of fleet size is measurable and extrapolable. AWS's own remediation is to add fine-grained alarming on thread consumption.

patterns.problem_and_mechanism: Scaling out crosses a limit that scales with fleet size rather than with load. evidence.citation: OpenAI incident, 11 December 2024

incidents.summary: A new telemetry service made every node run resource-intensive Kubernetes API operations whose cost scaled with cluster size. Although the data plane is designed to survive control-plane loss, the API server is required for DNS-based service discovery, so the decoupling did not hold. Engineers needed control-plane access to remove the service and could not get it.

Network control-plane jobs were descheduled by a rare maintenance event plus a bug allowing multiple independent clusters to be descheduled at once. The "fail static" defence held for minutes, not hours; configuration data was lost and had to be rebuilt. Debugging was hampered by tools competing over the congested network.

evidence.citation: Meta, More details about the October 4 outage

incidents.summary: A maintenance command disconnected the backbone; DNS servers withdrew their BGP announcements by design when they could not reach the data centres, so DNS went dark. Loss of DNS then broke the internal tooling engineers would have used to diagnose and fix it. Physical access was slow because facilities are hardened against modification.

observable_symptoms: Engineers report being unable to use standard tooling during the incident

evidence.citation: Cloudflare, Post-mortem on control plane and analytics outage

incidents.summary: Kafka and ClickHouse log processing existed only in the Portland PDX-04 facility while services in the three-facility Oregon HA cluster depended on them. Date of last successful DR exercise per product

evidence.citation: Joint statement from UniSuper and Google Cloud

incidents.summary: A joint statement attributes the event to "an inadvertent misconfiguration during provisioning of UniSuper's Private Cloud services" that resulted in deletion of the subscription. UniSuper ran duplicated systems in two geographic regions, but the deletion was at subscription level, so both went at once. Recovery was materially helped because "UniSuper had backups in place with an additional service provider".

Five regions spanning three different cloud providers, with no shared infrastructure, failed simultaneously because the base VM image carried a legacy automatic security-update channel whose default window is 06:00–07:00 UTC everywhere.

Cooling failure in a building hosting europe-west2-a during the UK heatwave; VM terminations and loss of machines for some customers. Oracle's London region reportedly suffered a cooling failure in the same heatwave — two independent providers, same weather.

leading_indicators.signal: Enumeration of objects shared across supposedly independent replicas — accounts, images, defaults, windows
Backups held with a different provider (presence or absence)

observable_symptoms: Simultaneous failure of environments with no shared infrastructure
Onset clustered at a vendor-default time
Both "redundant" copies gone at once
preconditions: A single account, subscription or contract object spanning all replicas
A common base image or configuration default
Geographic proximity within one weather or power system

known_limits: Environmental correlation (weather, power grid) requires external data most organisations do not model

remediations.failure_mode_if_wrong: Not an incident-time action
preconditions: Architectural change
remediations.verification: Confirm no single object spans all replicas

Base image provenance and enabled defaults per fleet

A legacy update channel and default window carried in a shared image

evidence.citation: npm blog, kik, left-pad and npm

Compromise reported by a third party rather than detected internally

Privileged access granted to third-party staff

evidence.citation: AWS, Summary of the Amazon DynamoDB Service Disruption, Sept 2015
Roblox return to service, 10/28–10/31 2021

incidents.summary: A brief network disruption caused storage servers to re-request membership data. Rapid GSI adoption had grown membership lists enough that requests approached the timeout threshold; requests timed out and retries compounded. Contributing factors AWS names include no monitoring on the membership-size dimension and insufficient metadata capacity. Escape required pausing metadata requests at 05:06 to shed load.

Consul, used for traffic routing and as a KV store, became the shared bottleneck; KV write latency p50 moved from under 300ms to 2s. Remediations included removing the Consul dependency from telemetry, sharding Consul and moving KV data elsewhere.

leading_indicators.signal: Per-request metadata payload size or membership-list size, trended
Metadata request latency as a fraction of the client timeout

observable_symptoms: Every dependent service degrading simultaneously
Metadata request latency approaching the client timeout
Recovery requiring deliberate load shedding at the metadata tier
preconditions: A single shared metadata service without cellular partitioning
A per-request cost dimension that grows with usage and is not monitored
Client caches refreshed infrequently, so a miss is expensive

known_limits: Requires the growth dimension to be instrumented; AWS's own postmortem cites its absence as a contributing factor
predictive_monitoring.rationale: The failure is a slow-growing per-request cost crossing a fixed timeout. Both quantities are observable and the crossing point is computable weeks ahead.

patterns.problem_and_mechanism: A service that every node consults for routing, membership or ownership information becomes the shared bottleneck. A transient fault causes many nodes to re-query it at once; a slow-growing dimension (membership list size, shard count) has quietly pushed per-request cost toward a timeout threshold; requests time out, nodes retry, and the metadata service is now the outage. remediations.blast_radius: All dependents operate on cached metadata
remediations.failure_mode_if_wrong: Clients with short cache lifetimes fail hard rather than degrading
preconditions: Clients tolerate stale metadata for the pause duration
remediations.verification: Metadata latency recovers; dependents stabilise

remediations.action: Add metadata capacity and partition the service into cells
remediations.failure_mode_if_wrong: Not an incident-time action
preconditions: Architectural change
remediations.verification: One cell's saturation no longer affects others

required_telemetry.signal: Membership/shard-map size per request

root_causes: Growth in a dimension nobody monitored — AWS names this explicitly for GSI-driven membership growth

evidence.citation: GitHub, October 21 post-incident analysis

Alquraan et al., OSDI '18 — 136 network-partitioning failures; 80% catastrophic; 90% silent

incidents.summary: Maintenance on failing 100G optical equipment severed connectivity for 43 seconds. Orchestrator nodes formed quorum on the West Coast and failed primaries over; on reconnection both sides held unreplicated writes. 24 hours 11 minutes of degradation. One busy cluster had 954 writes in the affected window; ~200,000 webhook payloads exceeded TTL and were dropped. The remediation was to prevent cross-region primary promotion.

leading_indicators.signal: Failover-system topology showing quorum achievable across a region boundary
Partition duration versus failover timeout

observable_symptoms: Two primaries in the topology
Application reads returning inconsistent results depending on which side is served
Replication unable to resume in either direction
preconditions: Automated failover triggered by timeout rather than by consensus

known_limits: Cannot predict the partition itself
Does not detect application-level inability to tolerate the post-promotion latency

patterns.problem_and_mechanism: A brief network partition causes an automated failover system to promote a new primary. When connectivity returns, both sides hold writes the other lacks, and there is no safe automatic merge. The fault lasts seconds; the recovery is bounded by data volume and manual reconciliation, so the outage is orders of magnitude longer than the fault. remediations.verification: Induced partition no longer produces cross-region promotion

evidence.citation: Monzo, Why Monzo wasn't working on July 29th

incidents.summary: Six new Cassandra nodes began serving reads for partitions before receiving the data, because of a misunderstanding of the auto_bootstrap flag's dual behaviour. ~9.5 hours; logins, payments, balances and in-app support all affected. Monzo states no monitoring existed for "row not found" errors that would have caught it faster, and that testing with one new node hid the bug because quorum masked it.

Rate of not-found or empty results, as a first-class metric separate from errors

observable_symptoms: Row not found or empty responses at normal latency and zero error rate
Users reporting missing data while dashboards are green
Inconsistency correlated with which node served the request

evidence.citation: GitLab, Postmortem of database outage of January 31

incidents.summary: During late-night remediation of a replication problem, an engineer ran a deletion command against the production cluster instead of the secondary, destroying ~300GB before it was killed. incidents.summary: Honeycomb documents that losing quorum on a Kafka topic partition left it unreadable for days, and that per-node recovery time had degraded from 8–12 hours to 48–72 hours, with an AZ-wide failure estimated at about a week. The remediation was a full platform migration.

evidence.citation: Cloudflare, How and why the leap second affected Cloudflare DNS

incidents.summary: RRDNS measured upstream resolver RTT with a wall-clock API. At the leap second the clock moved backward, producing a negative duration; the smoothed value was passed to a random function that panics on a negative argument. Peak ~0.2% of DNS queries; under 1% of HTTP requests errored. The panic was caught by the language runtime's recover mechanism, which escalated to engineers within 10 minutes. Fixed with a one-character change.

The leap-second adjustment did not notify the hrtimer subsystem that the clock had changed, so timeout calculations went wrong and futex-based waits timed out repeatedly, spinning CPU. Named affected processes in the thread include browsers, Java applications, virtualisation software and a database server. An Amadeus spokesperson confirmed to press that a kernel flaw caused an hour-long airline check-in outage, with a workaround applied within the hour.

evidence.citation: Microsoft, Summary of Windows Azure service disruption on Feb 29th, 2012

incidents.summary: A Guest Agent created a transfer certificate by adding one to the current year, producing 29 February 2013. Certificate creation failed and the agent terminated. The Host Agent waited 25 minutes for the handshake; three consecutive timeouts on a clean VM caused it to conclude a hardware fault and report the server, which was then service-healed onto another server where the bug reproduced. A second-order failure followed when the repair deployed an older Host Agent bundled with an incompatible networking plugin, taking down previously healthy services. 33% service credits were issued.
